fr:title.text: What a Verified zkVM Would Mean

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What a Verified zkVM Would Mean

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The statement at the top of the whole effort, written out honestly: which theorems compose, and which links in the chain are assumptions rather than proofs. It is the claim the whole effort will be judged on, and its general form is the issue of incorrect specification: a machine-checked proof is only ever as good as the statement it proves.

Questions this page should answer:
The chain: ISA specification, constraint system, arithmetisation soundness, IOP soundness, commitment security, Fiat–Shamir, recursion, extracted implementation.
Which links are proved today, which are stated, and which are not formalised at all.
The irreducible assumptions: hash security, conjectured proximity bounds, the compiler, the hardware.
Whether "verified" should mean the composed end-to-end theorem, or a set of component theorems with audited seams.
The 2027 target the project set, and what would have to be true for it to be met.
Sources: verified-zkevm.org, Verified-zkEVM overview.

The reason the rest of this corpus is organised the way it is. The verified zkEVM effort runs three tracks — the zkVM constraints, the EVM semantics, and the cryptography — and ArkLib and CompPoly are the cryptography track.

These pages stay closer to the code than the rest of the corpus, which also makes them the ones most likely to go stale. Related: protocol snarkification, computable specifications, formal verification in proof assistants.
A modular library of formally verified arguments of knowledge in Lean, organised around interactive oracle reductions rather than around individual protocols.

Questions this page should answer:
The directory structure as a design argument: OracleReduction, Commitments, ProofSystem, AGM, and the To* compatibility layers.
What is formalised and to what depth — sumcheck, Spartan, FRI, STIR, WHIR, Binius, Merkle trees, coding theory.
ProofSystem/ConstraintSystem: R1CS, Plonk, lookup, and memory checking in one place.
The security definitions in OracleReduction/Security, which are the real contribution.
What is a statement with no proof yet, and what the roadmap prioritises.
Which developments are blocked on CompPoly.
Sources: ArkLib, ArkLib on lean-lang.org.

Computable polynomials and finite fields in Lean: an executable mirror of the Mathlib definitions, with transfer theorems so proofs can be done on the noncomputable side. The case for computable specifications is made elsewhere; this page is about the artefact.

Questions this page should answer:
The representations chosen, and which operations each makes cheap. See univariate and multilinear polynomials.
The transfer pattern: computable definition, Mathlib definition, proven equivalence, and how proofs move across it.
Field representations and the small fields that matter — see the small-field turn.
What running the spec actually buys: testing a specification against a reference implementation.
Performance in Lean, and whether it is adequate for testing at realistic trace sizes.
Which ArkLib developments depend on it.

fr:title.text: Hash Functions in Bitcoin and Ethereum

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Hash Functions in Bitcoin and Ethereum

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Both major chains rest on a handful of hash functions, and which one is never only a cryptographic question. Bitcoin runs SHA-256 for proof of work, transaction identifiers, and its Merkle trees, with RIPEMD-160 alongside it for addresses. Ethereum runs Keccak for addresses, storage slots, and the state trie, and SHA-256 on the consensus layer — two families inside one protocol.

What has been in flux is a third kind of hash. For most of a decade the argument was that a proof system wants a function designed for it: an arithmetisation-friendly hash like Poseidon, whose round function is cheap counted in field multiplications rather than bit operations. On 13 August 2026 the Ethereum Foundation abandoned that direction for L1. Justin Drake's announcement is the primary source for all of this, and his one-line summary is the clearest statement of the reversal — "the key was not SNARK-friendly hashes, but hash-friendly SNARKs."

The reason is not that Poseidon broke. Proof systems over binary fields closed the gap from the other side, so a conventional hash is now cheap enough to prove that its decades of public cryptanalysis are the deciding factor. SHA-2 and the BLAKE family are the candidates, and which BLAKE — 2s or 3 — is not settled in anything published so far.

SHA-256, published by NIST in 2001, is a Merkle–Damgård construction over a 64-round compression function on 32-bit words, absorbing 64 bytes per call. It is the most analysed hash in deployment, and Bitcoin has used nothing else for its core since 2009.

Bitcoin applies it twice — \mathrm {SHA256}(\mathrm {SHA256}(x)), usually written SHA-256d — for block headers and so for proof of work, for transaction identifiers, and for the Merkle tree committing a block's transactions. The usual rationale for the second application is length extension: a Merkle–Damgård hash leaks enough internal state that an attacker who knows H(m) can compute H(m \| p) for some padding p without knowing m, and hashing the digest again removes the property.

Addresses use a second family as well. The legacy scheme hashes a public key with \mathrm {RIPEMD160}(\mathrm {SHA256}(x)), which shortens the digest to 20 bytes and means a break of either function alone does not immediately yield a preimage. Taproot's tagged hashes (BIP-340) are built from SHA-256 with a domain-separation prefix, so even the newest parts of Bitcoin stay inside the same primitive.

The conservatism is the design. Twenty-five years of public cryptanalysis with no practical attack on the full function is a stronger argument than any efficiency claim, and it is the argument the 2026 Ethereum decision came back around to.

Ethereum's workhorse is keccak256, and it is not SHA-3. Keccak won the NIST competition in 2012, NIST changed the padding rule before standardising it as FIPS 202 in 2015, and Ethereum had already shipped the original. The two differ in padding and produce different digests for the same input, which is a reliable source of confusion for anyone reimplementing an Ethereum client.

It is used almost everywhere state is named. An address is the last 20 bytes of the Keccak digest of a public key; a mapping's storage slot is the digest of the key concatenated with the slot number; Merkle–Patricia trie nodes are addressed by the digest of their RLP encoding; function selectors and event topics are digest prefixes; and the KECCAK256 opcode exposes it to contracts directly.

The consensus layer chose differently. SSZ's hash_tree_root is SHA-256, so a full node computes both families — Keccak for execution state and SHA-256 for beacon state. The EVM also exposes SHA-256 and RIPEMD-160 as precompiles at 0x02 and 0x03, and BLAKE2b's compression function at 0x09 (EIP-152, Istanbul, December 2019, priced at one gas per round).

For a prover this split matters, because the execution state is the Keccak half. Keccak is the most expensive of the three to prove — Flock reports 30k Keccak permutations per second per core against 42k SHA-256 compressions — though the gap per byte is narrower than the raw rates suggest, since one Keccak-256 permutation absorbs 136 bytes where a SHA-256 compression takes 64.

BLAKE was a SHA-3 finalist that lost to Keccak and then outlived the defeat. BLAKE2 (2013) cut the round count — 12 rounds where BLAKE had 16, or 10 where it had 14 — and dropped the HAIFA counter and constant additions for speed. BLAKE3 (2020) went further, to seven rounds, and replaced the serial mode with a tree.

The 2s and 2b split is a word-size split, and it is the detail that matters for the current Ethereum discussion.
BLAKE2b — 64-bit words, 1024-bit state, 128-byte blocks, 12 rounds, digests of any length from 1 to 64 bytes. Tuned for 64-bit CPUs.
BLAKE2s — 32-bit words, 512-bit state, 64-byte blocks, 10 rounds, digests of 1 to 32 bytes. Intended for 8- to 32-bit platforms, so it is the variant that suits constrained environments. Collision resistance follows the digest: up to 256 bits for 2b, up to 128 for 2s.

Both carry machinery that SHA-2 lacks. Keying is built into the compression function, so BLAKE2 is a MAC without needing HMAC around it, and the parameter block also takes a salt and a personalisation string, which gives domain separation for free rather than by convention. The family also includes parallel variants (BLAKE2sp, BLAKE2bp) and an extendable-output construction, BLAKE2X. In deployment, WireGuard uses BLAKE2s — 32-byte digests for hashing, keyed with 16-byte output as a MAC — and Zcash uses BLAKE2b for Equihash and for key derivation.

BLAKE3 keeps BLAKE2s's 32-bit words and 64-byte block and cuts to seven rounds, then splits the input into 1 KiB chunks arranged in a binary tree. That is what makes it parallel over any number of cores, incremental, and usable as an extendable-output function from a single algorithm rather than a family of them. The seven-round decision is the contested one: the designers argue the cryptanalysis supports it, and it is also the reason BLAKE3 has the least margin of anything in this note.

Which BLAKE Ethereum is actually considering is not yet public. Drake's announcement says "SHA or BLAKE"; some coverage reports the candidates as SHA-2 or BLAKE2s, other coverage says BLAKE3, and published benchmark comparisons put SHA-256, Keccak, BLAKE3 and leanXMSS side by side. The one thing that is clear is that the variant already in the EVM is not the one in question: EIP-152 exposes BLAKE2b's compression function at 0x09, added for Zcash interoperability, and BLAKE2b is the 64-bit variant that neither candidate set names.

My guess at the reasoning, which is inference and not something I have seen argued: for hash-based signatures the inputs are short and fixed-size, a 32-byte block at a time, so BLAKE3's chunking and tree mode buy nothing and only add constraints, while BLAKE2s gives the same 32-bit word size with three more rounds of margin and a decade of analysis. If the deciding workload is signature verification rather than hashing long messages, the tree is dead weight.
Sources: BLAKE2, the BLAKE3 specification draft, EIP-152.

fr:title.text: Poseidon, and Why Ethereum Walked Away

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Poseidon, and Why Ethereum Walked Away

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Poseidon (Grassi, Khovratovich, Rechberger, Roy, and Schofnegger, 2019) is a sponge over a prime field rather than over bits. Its permutation follows the HADES strategy: a few full rounds, where an S-box — typically x \mapsto x^5 — is applied to every element, and many partial rounds applying it to one, with an MDS matrix mixing the state between them. Poseidon2 later reworked the linear layer for speed. Because the whole function is field arithmetic, its cost inside a prime-field circuit is counted in multiplications, and it beat SHA-256 there by orders of magnitude.

The objection was always that the same algebraic structure that makes it cheap to arithmetise is what algebraic cryptanalysis attacks, and that parameters are generated per field and per state width rather than fixed once and studied for decades. The Ethereum Foundation took this seriously enough to fund the Poseidon Cryptanalysis Initiative, with bounties up to $1 million scheduled to run through December 2026.

It was paused on 1 August 2026, and on 13 August Justin Drake announced that the Foundation is abandoning Poseidon for L1 in favour of SHA or BLAKE, calling it "an epic 8-year, 8-figure rabbit hole in post-quantum cryptography" reaching "its dream conclusion." His diagnosis is the memorable part: "In hindsight the key was not SNARK-friendly hashes, but hash-friendly SNARKs."

What changed is the proving side. Binius moved the arithmetic into towers of binary fields, where a Boolean computation costs what it should instead of paying to embed single bits into a large prime field. Flock (eprint 2026/1329) took that further for the specific shape of the problem — large batches of the same Boolean circuit — and reports 82k BLAKE3 compressions, 42k SHA-256 compressions, and 30k Keccak permutations per second on one core of an M4 Max, more than 660k BLAKE3 compressions per second on ten, over 9 times faster than Binius64 on SHA-256 and more than 500 times faster than the fastest elliptic-curve SNARK it measured against. Drake's figure for the resulting designs is roughly one million conventional hash calls per second on a laptop, at about 100 times the cost of native execution.

Poseidon was not broken, and nothing here says it will be. An engineering decision was reversed because a different part of the stack improved, which is worth separating clearly from a cryptanalytic result — the security argument never changed, only what it had to buy. The stated roadmap puts a production-grade leanVM in 2027 and consensus, data, and execution layer deployment in 2028.
Sources: Drake's announcement, Flock and its implementation, the Poseidon Cryptanalysis Initiative.

The part that interests me is the second-order effect on verification. A conservative hash has a stable specification that many independent implementations already agree on, which matters a great deal if the goal is to verify an implementation rather than only a protocol. A generated parameter set does not offer that, whatever its cryptanalytic standing. The cost of hashing in a circuit is now one input to that decision rather than the whole of it.
Sources: Drake's announcement, the Poseidon Cryptanalysis Initiative, Flock.

Everything above, wrapped around an instruction set so that a program rather than a circuit is the thing being proved. A zkVM decomposes into three layers — the ISA, the VM architecture, and the proving layer — and most design disagreements are about where to put work between them.

This is the object the verified zkEVM effort is ultimately aimed at. A machine semantics in Lean is the first half of the statement one wants to prove about a zkVM; LC3 in Lean is that half at small scale.
A map of the layers, so that a claim about one system can be compared with a claim about another. Worth writing before the pages below it.

Questions this page should answer:
The three layers — ISA, VM architecture, proving layer — and the interface between each pair.
What "proving a program" means formally: the relation being proved, and where the program commitment enters.
Which layer a given optimisation belongs to, and which choices are genuinely independent.
The end-to-end statement a zkVM claims, written out in full.
Sources: SoK: Understanding zkVM, Projects that shaped modern zkVMs.

Whether to prove an existing ISA or design one for provability. RISC-V won the general-purpose end by bringing a compiler toolchain with it; the custom VMs argue the constraint cost is worth the loss.

Questions this page should answer:
RISC-V (RV32I and extensions) as a target: what makes each instruction class expensive to constrain.
Register machines versus stack machines (Miden, zkWasm), and what the memory argument looks like in each.
Purpose-built ISAs — Cairo, Valida — and the specific constraint-cost arguments for them.
Instruction decomposition and the lookup-based approach to semantics that Jolt takes.
The formal ISA specification: what the Sail-to-Lean route gives, and what it does not.
How an execution becomes a set of tables. In practice this is where a zkVM's engineering lives, and the details are what Clean has to be able to express.

Questions this page should answer:
Chips as separate AIRs, one per operation class, connected by cross-table lookups.
The main trace against auxiliary and preprocessed columns; what each costs to commit.
Padding to a power of two, and the constraints that must hold on padded rows.
Witness generation as a first-class cost, and whether the generator is verified against the constraints.
How a single instruction's semantics is spread across chips, and how the pieces are tied back together.

Random-access memory is the hardest part of a zkVM to constrain and the most common source of unsoundness. The general machinery is in permutation and memory arguments; this page is about what the systems actually do.

Questions this page should answer:
Read-write RAM by offline memory checking, as in SP1, Jolt, and RISC Zero.
Paged memory with Merkle verification, which RISC Zero also supports, and when that is preferable.
Stack-based models (Miden, zkWasm) and how their consistency arguments differ.
Memory across shard boundaries — the argument that ties independent segments together.
The concrete cost of a load or store, counted in trace cells and lookups.
Sources: SoK: Understanding zkVM, Nebula.

Hand-written circuits for hot operations — hashes, elliptic-curve arithmetic, big-integer work — invoked from the VM instead of being proved instruction by instruction. Large speedups, and a large increase in the amount of hand-written constrained code that has to be correct.

Questions this page should answer:
The mechanism: how a precompile attaches to the trace and how its inputs and outputs are tied to VM state.
The speedups claimed, and on which workloads they decide the benchmark.
The soundness surface: an under-constrained precompile is a complete break, with no compiler to catch it.
Extensibility as a design goal, and what a user-supplied precompile has to prove.
Why this is the most valuable place in the stack to point Clean at.
One entry per system: backend, arithmetisation, field, memory model, and the choice that distinguishes it. The point is a comparison table, not a survey.

Questions this page should answer:
SP1 — RISC-V on Plonky3, precompile-heavy.
Jolt — Lasso-based, lookups for instruction semantics, notably small proofs.
RISC Zero — RISC-V, read-write and paged Merkle memory.
OpenVM — modular and extensible by construction; what its extension interface requires.
Stwo and Cairo — circle STARKs over Mersenne31, with a purpose-built ISA.
Miden and Valida — stack machine and provability-first ISA respectively.
For each: what its soundness rests on that the others' does not.
Sources: SoK: Understanding zkVM, sp1, jolt, risc0, openvm, awesome-zkvm.
What actually costs time, and how to read a published comparison. The target is a cost model good enough to predict the direction of a change before measuring it.

Questions this page should answer:
The cost breakdown: witness generation, hashing, FFTs, MSMs, extension-field arithmetic.
Cycles per second as a metric, and what it hides — precompiles, shard size, security parameters.
Proof size and verifier time across systems, and the recursion that produces the final numbers.
How the field choice shows up in measurements, and why hash rate is often the real headline.
Comparing at equal security: the benchmark question that is usually skipped.
Sources: zkvm-benchmarks.

A catalogue of real failure modes, kept concrete. This page is the evidence for the formalisation work, so it should stay evidence rather than argument. Smart contract vulnerabilities due to poor specification is the same catalogue one domain over, and the failure modes rhyme: code that did what it was specified to do, and a specification that permitted what nobody intended.

Questions this page should answer:
Under-constrained circuits: the general shape, and the canonical examples.
Missing range checks, and why a forgotten monotonicity constraint on memory timestamps is fatal.
Fiat–Shamir misuse: transcripts missing a value, weak domain separation, insufficient challenge space.
Soundness bugs in published schemes rather than implementations — Nova is the example to write up.
Parameter errors: a security level computed in the wrong regime.
Which of these a type system, a linter, an audit, or a proof would each have caught.
Sources: how Nova got broken, How to Prove False Statements.

Poseidon2 later reworked the linear layer for speed. Because the whole function is field arithmetic, its cost inside a prime-field circuit is counted in multiplications, and it beat SHA-256 there by orders of magnitude.

The objection was always that the same algebraic structure that makes it cheap to arithmetise is what algebraic cryptanalysis attacks, and that parameters are generated per field and per state width rather than fixed once and studied for decades. The Ethereum Foundation took this seriously enough to fund the Poseidon Cryptanalysis Initiative, with bounties up to $1 million scheduled to run through December 2026.

It was paused on 1 August 2026, and on 13 August Justin Drake announced that the Foundation is abandoning Poseidon for L1 in favour of SHA or BLAKE, calling it "an epic 8-year, 8-figure rabbit hole in post-quantum cryptography" reaching "its dream conclusion." His diagnosis is the memorable part: "In hindsight the key was not SNARK-friendly hashes, but hash-friendly SNARKs."

What changed is the proving side. Binius moved the arithmetic into towers of binary fields, where a Boolean computation costs what it should instead of paying to embed single bits into a large prime field. Flock (eprint 2026/1329) took that further for the specific shape of the problem — large batches of the same Boolean circuit — and reports 82k BLAKE3 compressions, 42k SHA-256 compressions, and 30k Keccak permutations per second on one core of an M4 Max, more than 660k BLAKE3 compressions per second on ten, over 9 times faster than Binius64 on SHA-256 and more than 500 times faster than the fastest elliptic-curve SNARK it measured against. Drake's figure for the resulting designs is roughly one million conventional hash calls per second on a laptop, at about 100 times the cost of native execution.

Poseidon was not broken, and nothing here says it will be. An engineering decision was reversed because a different part of the stack improved, which is worth separating clearly from a cryptanalytic result — the security argument never changed, only what it had to buy. The stated roadmap puts a production-grade leanVM in 2027 and consensus, data, and execution layer deployment in 2028.
Sources: Drake's announcement, Flock and its implementation, the Poseidon Cryptanalysis Initiative.

The part that interests me is the second-order effect on verification. A conservative hash has a stable specification that many independent implementations already agree on, which matters a great deal if the goal is to verify an implementation rather than only a protocol. A generated parameter set does not offer that, whatever its cryptanalytic standing. The cost of hashing in a circuit is now one input to that decision rather than the whole of it.
Sources: Drake's announcement, the Poseidon Cryptanalysis Initiative, Flock.

fr:title.text: Soundness Regimes and the Proximity-Gap Conjectures

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Soundness Regimes and the Proximity-Gap Conjectures

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The same protocol has different soundness depending on how far from the code you are willing to reason, and the parameters used in production sit in the regime where the analysis is conjectural. This page is the reason list decoding is in this corpus at all.

Questions this page should answer:
Unique decoding, the Johnson bound, and capacity: the guarantee each yields and the parameters each licenses.
What must be conjectured to reach capacity, and the precise statement of each conjecture.
Threshold halving, and what it establishes above the Johnson bound.
The accounting from soundness error to bits of security, including grinding.
Which deployed systems set parameters in which regime — and whether the choice is documented anywhere citable.
Sources: SoK: Hash-Based Polynomial Commitments, On Reed–Solomon Proximity Gaps Conjectures, FRI Soundness Above the Johnson Bound.

fr:title.text: Proof Assistants and the Issue of Incorrect Specification

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Proof Assistants and the Issue of Incorrect Specification

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Proof assistants give us a formal and robustly mathematical environment in which to prove mathematical theorems and arbitrary properties of programs. Virtually anything that can be stated; true propositions can all in principle be proved. You would think that this would make proof assistants the silver bullet to software security: Since you could truly state and prove any desirable security or performance property, if the tools are good enough you might think that they are precisely what's needed to make high-assurance software absolutely bullet-proof. The reality is, however, it is difficult to write a complete specification; desirable properties of some software can be extremely difficult to articulate.

Some software will need a great deal of formal infrastructure built up to write provably correct specifications. For others, it's not even obvious that formal statements are the right tool to use for them. Computer science has a long history of using diagrams, pictures, and other tools of abstraction to specify computation. Maybe a proof assistant is powerful enough to formalize any abstract framework? Maybe it's powerful enough to do this? If it is, how do we proceed? How do we coax that power out so that all desirable properties of software can be clearly articulated, specified and ultimately formally proved?
